name: Methyltestosterone

lead: Methyltestosterone is one of the earliest orally active forms of testosterone. It has been used for male hypogonadism, in women with estrogens for menopausal symptoms, and in hereditary angioedema; the payoff relevant to looks is androgen replacement, which supports muscle and masculine traits.

It is testosterone with a methyl group at the 17-alpha position, which allows oral dosing and acts on the androgen receptor. No trial has tested it for muscle or facial appearance, and no community threads about it were found. The most relevant human study is a 1993 NIH trial in healthy men that measured mood and behavior effects over two weeks.

paras: Medically it is taken as an oral tablet, in men for hypogonadism and in women as combination estrogen-methyltestosterone tablets for menopausal symptoms. It is not a common choice in bodybuilding or looksmaxxing circles.

Reported risks include virilization in women, liver toxicity, mood changes and a drug interaction with cyclosporine. Combination estrogen-methyltestosterone tablets carry a boxed warning about endometrial cancer risk and are Pregnancy Category X. It is prohibited in sport.

angle.text: Methyltestosterone is an oral testosterone analogue that raises androgen levels, which supports muscle and masculine traits in men with hypogonadism. Medical use covers hypogonadism and menopausal therapy; it is rarely discussed for physique.

lead: Methyltestosterone is a synthetic androgen and anabolic steroid: testosterone with an added methyl group at the 17-alpha position, which lets it be taken by mouth. In appearance terms it belongs to the family of androgens that increase muscle, body hair and other male secondary sexual characteristics, and Wikipedia and Grokipedia both note that athletes and bodybuilders have used it for strength and muscle, although less commonly than other steroids. [1][2][3]

It was first synthesized in 1935 by Leopold Ruzicka's group in Zurich and introduced for medical use in 1936, making it one of the earliest synthetic androgens and the first 17-alpha-alkylated one. [1][2] Medically it has been used in men for hypogonadism and delayed puberty, in women for advanced breast cancer and, combined with esterified estrogens, for menopausal symptoms. [1][4][5][6]

Published human trials cover hereditary angioedema, menopausal hormone therapy and a 1993 NIH study of mood and behavior in healthy men; none has measured muscle or facial appearance in healthy people. [7][8][9] Regulators treat it as a controlled substance in several countries and sport authorities prohibit it. [1][2]
infobox: Oral; buccal or sublingual forms exist [1]
Android, Metandren, Testred, Methitest; with esterified estrogens: Estratest, Covaryx, Essian [1][11]
US Schedule III; UK Class C; Canada Schedule IV; Australia S4 [1][2]

paras: In males, Wikipedia lists delayed puberty, hypogonadism, cryptorchidism and erectile dysfunction as uses or former uses, and says the US approval covers hypogonadism and delayed puberty in males and inoperable breast cancer in females. [1] Reviews of hypogonadism therapy discuss oral and alternative androgens alongside conventional testosterone replacement. [5] Grokipedia adds palliation of advanced hormone-responsive breast cancer and postpartum breast engorgement in women. [2]

In women, androgen therapy has been used mainly to improve sexual function after menopause, and reviews discuss testosterone's role in female sexuality and well-being and the lack of an established clinical definition of deficiency. [6][10] A combination of esterified estrogens and methyltestosterone is indicated on its US label for moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms not improved by estrogens alone. [4] That combination was first marketed in the US in 1965 under the brand Estratest and its manufacturer announced discontinuation of Estratest in March 2009, though other branded versions exist. [11]

Randomized studies in postmenopausal women examined vasodilator effects, circulating hormone levels, stress cardiovascular responses and bone density with combined estrogen-androgen therapy. [12][13][14][15] A double-blind trial found methyltestosterone effective in preventing hereditary angioedema attacks. [7]

Grokipedia states that methyltestosterone is misused by athletes and bodybuilders to increase strength and muscle and is banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency at all times; Wikipedia similarly says non-medical use by athletes and bodybuilders occurs but is less common than for other anabolic steroids. [2][1] Wikipedia's anabolic steroid article notes that many users of such compounds are non-competitive lifters who use them for cosmetic reasons. [3]

Androgens in general act on the androgen receptor, and Wikipedia reports that methyltestosterone's androgenic-to-anabolic ratio is roughly 1:1, similar to testosterone, with notable estrogenic activity because it converts to an estrogenic metabolite. [1] No controlled trial has tested methyltestosterone for muscle, body composition, skin or facial outcomes in healthy people.

Randomized studies include a double-blind trial in four hereditary angioedema patients, an eight-week crossover trial adding methyltestosterone to estrogen in menopausal women, further trials of combined estrogen-androgen therapy in postmenopausal women, and a two-week NIH placebo-controlled crossover trial of mood and behavior in 20 healthy men. [7][8][12][13][14][9] Registered trials found for related products concern testosterone undecanoate and other formulations, not methyltestosterone. No trial has examined appearance outcomes.

In the 1977 hereditary angioedema study, patients taking methyltestosterone had four attacks over 46 cumulative months compared with 19 episodes over 11.8 months on placebo. [7] In menopausal women already on estrogen, adding methyltestosterone for eight weeks significantly improved a complex attention test but not other tests, and the overall score did not change on average. [8]

In the 1993 NIH trial, healthy male volunteers took methyltestosterone in a fixed-order, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover over two weeks while mood and behavior were rated on an inpatient unit. [9]

Wikipedia lists androgenic effects including acne, body-hair growth, voice changes and increased libido, estrogenic effects including fluid retention and gynecomastia, possible liver toxicity with extended use, increased red blood cell production at high doses with thrombosis risk, and aggression or psychiatric symptoms at very high doses. It says women and children face risk of irreversible virilization and that estrogenic activity can accelerate growth-plate closure in children. It is contraindicated in men with prostate cancer. [1]

Grokipedia describes cholestatic jaundice, peliosis hepatis and hepatic tumors as serious liver effects associated with prolonged high-dose use of 17-alpha-alkylated androgens, notes that cholestatic jaundice was reported as early as 1947, and says use declined from the 1970s over hepatotoxicity concerns. [2] Wikipedia's anabolic steroid article similarly attributes liver injury risks mostly to 17-alpha-alkylated compounds. [3] A 1964 report described iatrogenic precocious puberty, and a 1991 case report described an interaction with cyclosporine. [16][17]

The US label of the estrogen-methyltestosterone combination carries a boxed warning about endometrial carcinoma, is Pregnancy Category X, and lists estrogen-associated adverse effects including thromboembolism and gallbladder disease. [4]

Methyltestosterone is an androgen receptor agonist. Wikipedia reports it is converted by 5-alpha-reductase to a more potent androgen and aromatized to an estrogen, and that it lowers sex hormone-binding globulin. [1] Grokipedia adds that it suppresses gonadotropins through negative feedback. [2] In a laboratory study, testosterone, methyltestosterone and epitestosterone at physiological concentrations protected human primary neurons from serum-deprivation-induced apoptosis through the androgen receptor. [18]

The 17-alpha methyl group slows hepatic breakdown, which is why the compound works orally, unlike plain testosterone. [1][3] Wikipedia gives oral bioavailability of about 70% and a half-life near 2.5 to 3 hours, with most of the dose excreted in urine; Grokipedia gives roughly 50% bioavailability and 2.5 to 3.5 hours, so figures differ between sources. [1][2] Buccal or sublingual use is reported to increase bioavailability. [1]

The compound is 17-alpha-methylandrost-4-en-17-beta-ol-3-one, formula C20H30O2, molar mass about 302 g/mol. [1] It is the parent structure of the 17-alpha-alkylated class, which includes metandienone and fluoxymesterone. [1]

Methyltestosterone was synthesized in 1935 alongside methandriol and mestanolone, with the work attributed to Ruzicka, Goldberg and Rosenberg in Helvetica Chimica Acta, and was introduced medically in 1936. [1] Grokipedia says early clinical reports in 1938 described oral efficacy and that capon comb assays showed activity by mouth. [2] The combination with esterified estrogens was first marketed in the US in 1965. [11] A 2003 safety surveillance review of that combination covering 1989 to 2002 reported a relatively small number of serious adverse events. [11]

Physicians in the 1930s onward used anabolic-androgenic steroids for many purposes with varied success, and the later spread of such steroids into sport and physique culture is documented in Wikipedia's anabolic steroid article. [3]

Wikipedia reports methyltestosterone is a Schedule III controlled substance in the United States, Schedule IV in Canada and prescription-only (S4) in Australia; Grokipedia lists Class C in the UK under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 and notes the 1990 US Anabolic Steroids Control Act as the basis for US scheduling. [1][2] WADA prohibits it at all times, and Grokipedia reports that about 1% of anabolic-agent adverse analytical findings in sport in 2003 to 2018 involved it. [2]

Methyltestosterone is mentioned in discussions of oral steroids, but encyclopedia sources describe it as less commonly used non-medically than other anabolic steroids. [1] No community threads specifically about its appearance effects were identified in the sources for this article.

Methyltestosterone is widely used in aquaculture research to produce all-male fish stocks, and studies in zebrafish, flounder and fathead minnow describe its effects on gonad development and aromatase expression; it has also been measured as an environmental steroid in wastewater. [19][20][21][22][23] These studies concern animals and the environment, not human appearance.
